SEC17A-01.note: In 'not X but Y' the verb agrees with Y (sweep, singular); the delayed object 'the bat's path' requires active voice. 'were steering' is pulled by the plural 'ears' sitting closer in 'not the ears but'.

SEC17A-02.note: 'every X and every Y' takes a singular verb, and 'Since ... was written' demands present perfect. 'have been recording' tempts anyone who treats the and-compound as plural.

SEC17A-03.note: Subject 'such a lens' is singular and is acted on (no object follows), so singular passive. 'are transported' is attracted by the long fronted modifier's plurals (prisms, workshops, frames); 'transports' is semantically absurd.

SEC17A-04.note: Relative 'that' takes the compound 'the skull and the lower jaw' (confirmed by 'their ... each other'): plural; past narrative and the later removal rule out 'are lying'. 'has lain' tempts readers who attach 'that' to 'jaw' alone.

SEC17A-05.note: Inverted 'So uneven were the measurements ... that': subject is plural 'measurements', and the past frame plus 'have since brought the readings into range' excludes present 'are'. 'was'/'has been' tempt via the singular 'hall's' near the verb.

SEC17A-06.note: 'as do' substitutes for the predicate 'hold back ... and release'; the inverted subject 'trumpets' is plural. 'as does' is pulled by the singular-sounding 'species'/'tobacco'; 'as is' / 'as are' fail because a be-form cannot stand in for an action verb phrase.

SEC17A-07.note: Fronted predicate inversion: subject is singular 'collapse'; 'to the present day' requires present perfect, which also rules out 'was once' (implies it is no longer puzzling). 'were once'/'have been' are attracted by 'specialists' directly before the blank.

SEC17A-08.note: The transposition happened before the astronomer 'found' it (past), so past perfect. 'has transposed' is the main lure for readers who see a completed action without anchoring to the past reporting verb; 'transposes' is clearly wrong for a dead compiler.

SEC17A-09.note: An introductory 'Although' clause is joined to the main clause with a comma; semicolon and colon need an independent clause before them. No punctuation (D) is the strongest lure because 'spot a laser gauge' reads on.

SEC17A-10.note: Two independent clauses joined by the conjunctive adverb 'however' need a semicolon before it and a comma after; 'however' belongs to the contrasting second clause, not the first (C). D is a comma splice; B's colon before 'however' is non-standard.

SEC17B-01.note: In 'the only one of the visitors that', the relative clause refers to 'one', so singular; the object 'pollen' (after the interrupter) requires active voice. 'are carrying' is the strongest lure via 'visitors' directly before 'that'.

SEC17B-02.note: In the cleft 'it is the juvenile shells ... that', the verb agrees with 'shells' (plural), and shells are acted on (passive). 'is misidentified' tempts readers who agree with the cleft's 'it is'.

SEC17B-03.note: Singular subject 'photoperiod' with a delayed object 'the week' requires singular active; 'across those decades' fits present perfect. 'have determined' is pulled by 'botanists and climatologists'/'decades'; the passives fail because an object follows.

SEC17B-04.note: 'more than one core' takes a singular verb, and the completed 'Until the team switched' window requires simple past, excluding 'has been'. 'have been in pieces' is the intuitive notional plural.

SEC17B-05.note: 'Not until ...' triggers do-support inversion; the subject 'eggs' is plural and the frame is present ('refill', habitual), so 'do the'. 'does' is attracted by the stack of singular adjectives/'silt'; 'did' needs the present to be noticed; 'is the' fails with bare 'hatch'.

SEC17B-06.note: Fronted participle inversion: the subject is singular 'account', and the past frame ('bore', 'has since transferred') excludes 'is' and 'has been' (it is no longer bundled). 'were evidently' is attracted by 'envelopes' right before the blank.

SEC17B-07.note: Inverted 'Such has been the pressure ... that': the subject is singular 'pressure'; 'ever since' plus present 'now survives' requires present perfect, excluding 'had been' and 'is now'. 'have been' is pulled by 'goat herds'/'farmers' later in the subject phrase.

SEC17B-08.note: A forecast reported with present perfect 'has announced' and tied to 'once the chamber is refilled' takes future 'will'. 'would remain' is the lure, for readers who apply backshift as if the reporting verb were simple past.

SEC17B-09.note: The subject 'pigment' carries a reduced relative clause ('the illuminators ... ground by hand from imported lapis lazuli') and then the main verb 'cost'. No punctuation belongs between subject and verb. The comma tempts because the long modifier feels like it needs closing, and 'ground' garden-paths the reader.

SEC17B-10.note: The colon introduces the 'one thing' that was feared; the semicolon fails because 'a single heavy rain ...' is not an independent clause. The comma (B) is the strongest lure, as an end appositive, but it would attach the phrase to 'prices' rather than 'one thing'. Closest call in the batch.

tells: Attractor-noun scheme is near-uniform in the agreement items: the noun closest to the blank disagrees in number with the true subject (A-01 ears, A-03 frames, A-07 specialists, B-01 visitors, B-03 botanists/decades, B-06 envelopes, B-07 herds). A test-taker who simply picks the number OPPOSITE the nearest noun gets most of these without finding the subject; it fails only on A-02, B-02, B-04, A-04.

Singular keys dominate the agreement items (A-01, A-02, A-03, A-07, B-01, B-03, B-04, B-06, B-07 = 9 singular vs A-04, A-05, A-06, B-02, B-05 = 5 plural). The 'pick singular when the subject looks plural' bias pays off.

Active/passive axis in the 2x2 grids (A-01, A-03, B-01, B-02, B-03) is always settled by whether an object follows the interrupter, with the same delayed-object-after-commas construction in A-01, B-01, B-03.

Tense axis: whenever a durative anchor appears ('Since', 'to the present day', 'ever since', 'across those decades') the present-perfect option is the key (A-02, A-07, B-07, B-03); whenever a completed past window appears it is simple/past perfect (A-08, B-04, B-06). That is the rule itself rather than a tell, but the anchor is always conspicuously planted.
Punctuation items: no mark is always the key (comma A-09, semicolon+however A-10, none B-09, colon B-10). No positional tell observed; my answer letters spread A6/B4/C5/D5.

No item has a resolving word within four words after the blank: interrupters are placed after the blank consistently (A-01, A-04, B-01, B-03), a construction that itself becomes recognisable across the batch.
near_duplicates: so/such + adjective/predicate inversion with 'that' result clause; agreement plus tense
fronted predicate/participle inversion, singular subject after a plural attractor, tense from a later clause
singular subject, active voice with object delayed by a comma interrupter, plural noun earlier in the sentence
same 2x2 grid (was/were x active/passive), delayed object after a comma interrupter
agreement inside a relative/cleft 'that' clause with a plural noun just before 'that'
quantified-subject singular rule ('every X and every Y', 'more than one') combined with a tense anchor
inversion after a fronted negative/degree phrase, plural subject, tense from context

phase2_note: All 20 keys match my cold answers, and every authored explanation produces its key and accounts for each distractor. Minor wording points that do not change the verdict: on B-10 the explanation says the comma reading adds a third feared item, but the stronger objection is that it attaches the phrase to 'prices' as an appositive; it is still the closest distractor in the batch. On A-08, 'was transposing' is better rejected as aspectually wrong for a completed error than as 'at the time of the discovery'. No per-item drop. These are form-composition cautions, not drops: A-01, B-01 and B-03 share the same was/were x active/passive grid with a delayed object, and A-05 and B-07 share the so/such inversion, so avoid putting a pair on one form. Across the agreement items the nearest noun mismatches the subject's number in most cases (see the summary tells).
